title: Committee to Protect and Preserve the Idaho Constitution v. State of Idaho
description: Whether the Idaho parental choice tax credit, which provides refundable tax credits for private educational services, violates the Idaho Constitution by creating a separate, publicly funded education system or by primarily benefiting private interests rather than a public purpose.
plaintiff_argument: The petitioners argued that the tax credit violates Article IX, section 1 of the Idaho Constitution by indirectly funding private schools, thereby creating a separate system of nonpublic education, and also violates the "public purpose doctrine" by primarily benefiting private entities.
defendant_argument: The respondents argued that the petitioners lacked standing, that Article IX, section 1 of the Idaho Constitution sets a floor, not a ceiling, for legislative power regarding education, and that the tax credit serves a public purpose by facilitating parental choice in educational services.
decision_outcome: The court denied the Petitioners' request for a writ of prohibition, finding the Idaho parental choice tax credit constitutional.

title: State v. Fletcher
description: Whether exterior sniffs of a vehicle by a drug dog constitute a search under Article 1, Section 17 of the Idaho Constitution, and whether Article 1, Section 17 imposes a heightened standard for the automobile exception to the warrant requirement.
plaintiff_argument: Fletcher argued that drug dog sniffs should be considered searches under Idaho's Constitution and that Article 1, Section 17 provides greater protection for vehicle searches, requiring a warrant even with the automobile exception when practicable.
defendant_argument: The State argued that drug dog sniffs are not searches, that Idaho's Constitution does not provide heightened protection for the automobile exception, and that the automobile exception applied, especially given Fletcher's probation waiver.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the district court's denial of Fletcher's motion to suppress, ruling that exterior drug dog sniffs are not searches under the Idaho Constitution and declining to impose a heightened standard for the automobile exception.

title: Idahoans United for Women & Families v. Labrador
description: Whether the Fiscal Impact Statement (FIS) and ballot titles for the "Reproductive Freedom and Privacy Act" citizen initiative substantially comply with Idaho law, with the plaintiff arguing they do not and the defendants arguing they do.
plaintiff_argument: Idahoans United argued that the Fiscal Impact Statement (FIS) lacked a factual basis, was unclear, and used unnecessary legal terms, and that the short ballot title was not distinctive or comprehensive and used prejudicial language, thus failing to comply with Idaho law.
defendant_argument: The Idaho Division of Financial Management (DFM) and the Attorney General argued that the FIS and ballot titles substantially complied with Idaho law, and that DFM had discretion in determining the FIS content, while the Attorney General's use of "fetus viability" in the short ballot title was common and not prejudicial.
decision_outcome: The court dismissed the petition against the Secretary of State, partially granted the writ of mandamus against the Idaho Division of Financial Management (DFM) for the Fiscal Impact Statement (FIS) and against the Attorney General for the short ballot title, and denied the writ of mandamus for the long ballot title, ordering DFM and the Attorney General to provide revised documents.

title: State v. Pulizzi
description: Whether a city's waste collection ordinance creates an objectively reasonable expectation of privacy in curbside garbage, thereby protecting it from warrantless searches under the Fourth Amendment and Idaho Constitution Article I, section 17.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the district court correctly determined the Twin Falls City waste collection ordinance did not create an objectively reasonable expectation of privacy, and that existing precedent holds there is no reasonable expectation of privacy in curbside trash.
defendant_argument: Pulizzi argued he had a reasonable expectation of privacy in his curbside garbage because the city's waste collection ordinances mandated participation and restricted who could collect garbage, thus violating his Fourth Amendment and Idaho Constitution rights, and that prior holdings should be reconsidered.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed Pulizzi's judgment of conviction, ruling that the Twin Falls City waste collection ordinance did not create an objectively reasonable expectation of privacy in curbside garbage.

title: Murray v. Dalton (In re Doe)
description: Whether the guardianship of Jane Doe by her grandparents should be terminated, considering the biological mother's claims of unconstitutional guardianship statutes and parental alienation, versus the grandparents' arguments regarding the mother's unfitness and the constitutionality of the laws.
plaintiff_argument: Alayna A. Dalton argued that Idaho's guardianship laws unconstitutionally infringe on fundamental parental rights, that the lower court's finding of her unfitness was erroneous, and that the Murrays' parental alienation warranted termination of the guardianship.
defendant_argument: Robert Timothy Murray and Teena Marie Murray argued that the Idaho Parental Rights Act does not apply to private guardianships, Alayna waived her right to challenge certain statutes, the statutes are constitutional, Alayna was an unfit parent, and their actions did not constitute parental alienation.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the magistrate court's decision to deny Alayna A. Dalton's petition to terminate the guardianship.

title: State v. Barr
description: Whether Idaho Code section 19-2520G(3), which mandates consecutive sentences, violates the Idaho Constitution's separation of powers by usurping the judiciary's authority to determine whether sentences run consecutively or concurrently.
plaintiff_argument: Barr argued that the mandatory consecutive sentence requirement violates the Idaho Constitution's separation of powers by usurping the judiciary's inherent power to determine whether a sentence runs consecutively or concurrently, and that Article V, section 13 does not empower the legislature to mandate consecutive sentences.
defendant_argument: The State contended that the phrase "mandatory minimum sentence" includes the ability to mandate consecutive sentences, and that at common law, judicial authority to impose consecutive sentences was subject to statutory limitation, meaning this power was not exclusively reserved to the judiciary.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the district court's decision denying Barr's Rule 35(a) motion, ruling that the power to designate whether a criminal sentence be served concurrently or consecutively is not one reserved exclusively to the judiciary at common law, and therefore Idaho Code section 19-2520G(3) does not violate the separation of powers.

title: BABE VOTE v. McGrane
description: Whether House Bills 124 and 340, which modified acceptable forms of identification for voter registration and voting at polls, violate the Idaho Constitution's guarantee of equal protection and unduly burden the right of suffrage.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that House Bills 124 and 340 violate the Idaho Constitution's guarantee of equal protection and unduly burden the right of suffrage, particularly for young voters and out-of-state students, by making it more difficult to register and vote.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the bills impose minimal burdens, do not classify based on age or suspect class, and were enacted with a rational basis, thus not violating the Idaho or United States Constitutions.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the district court's decision, ruling that House Bills 124 and 340 are reasonable exercises of the legislature's authority to enact conditions on the right of suffrage and do not violate the Idaho Constitution's equal protection clause.

title: Worthington v. Thunder
description: Whether a tenant has a constitutional right to a jury trial in an unlawful detainer action, and whether Idaho Code section 6-311A, which mandates a bench trial for such actions, violates the Idaho Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The Worthingtons argued that an unlawful detainer action is an equitable claim for possession of property, not a legal claim for money damages, and therefore does not entitle the defendant to a jury trial under the Idaho Constitution. They also argued that Idaho Code section 6-311A is constitutional.
defendant_argument: Crazy Thunder argued that she has a constitutional right to a jury trial for the legal claims raised in her affirmative defenses in the unlawful detainer action, and that Idaho Code section 6-311A, if interpreted to deny this right, violates the Idaho Constitution.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the district court's decision that Crazy Thunder was entitled to a jury trial, but on different grounds. The Court held that Idaho Code section 6-311A is constitutional when no issues of fact are presented, but when a defendant raises legal claims through affirmative defenses, the right to a jury trial under Idaho Code section 6-313 and the Idaho Constitution remains inviolate.

title: Idaho State Athletic Commission v. Office of the Administrative Rules Coordinator
description: Whether the legislative preapproval provisions of the Idaho Administrative Procedure Act, particularly for administrative fee rules, violate the Idaho Constitution, and whether the Rules Coordinator has a clear legal duty to publish the Athletic Commission's 2022 Rules without such approval.
plaintiff_argument: The petitioners argued that the legislative preapproval provisions of the APA are unconstitutional, violating separation of powers, enactment, presentment, and Article III, section 29 of the Idaho Constitution, and therefore the Rules Coordinator had a clear legal duty to publish their 2022 Rules.
defendant_argument: The respondents argued that the Rules Coordinator was statutorily bound not to publish rules without legislative approval, and the intervenor (Idaho Legislature) contended that the preapproval provisions are constitutional and that temporary rulemaking provides an adequate alternative remedy.
decision_outcome: The court dismissed the Petition for a declaratory judgment and denied the Petition for a writ of mandamus, ruling that the legislative preapproval provisions are constitutional.

title: State v. Oldenburg
description: Whether Idaho Code section 67-3004(10) independently grants lower courts the authority to seal criminal court files, or if this power rests exclusively with the Idaho Supreme Court through its administrative rules.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff, Nickolaus Oldenburg, argued that the 2018 amendments to Idaho Code section 67-3004(10) act on their own to expand the basis for sealing Idaho court records, providing a broader category of defendants the ability to seal their underlying criminal case.
defendant_argument: The defendant, State of Idaho, argued that Idaho Code section 67-3004(10) cannot operate independently because it would be an impermissible overreach into the authority vested in the Idaho Supreme Court by Article V, section 13, of the Idaho Constitution, violating the separation of powers.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the district court's order, concluding that the district court did not have the authority to seal Oldenburg's court records pursuant to Idaho Code section 67-3004(10) because the legislature cannot independently vest such authority.

title: State v. Harrell
description: Whether the district court erred in denying Harrell's motion to suppress evidence and in denying his objection to the reduction of peremptory challenges.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the officer had reasonable suspicion to expand the traffic stop and probable cause for the search, and that the number of peremptory challenges is a procedural, not substantive, right, which the Court had inherent power to modify.
defendant_argument: Harrell argued that the extended traffic stop and warrantless search violated his Fourth Amendment rights and that both the Idaho and U.S. Constitutions guarantee him ten peremptory challenges, making the reduction an error.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Idaho affirmed Harrell's judgment of conviction, ruling that the district court did not err in denying his motion to suppress or his objection to the reduction of peremptory challenges.

title: Tidwell v. Blaine County
description: Whether Kiki Leslie A. Tidwell and the Madison Jean Tidwell Qualified Subchapter S Trust had standing to challenge Blaine County's decision to allow affordable housing on Parcel C, with plaintiffs arguing they had standing due to potential property value diminution and recreational interests, and defendants arguing plaintiffs lacked particularized injury.
plaintiff_argument: Plaintiffs argued they had standing because the proposed development would diminish their property values, impair their aesthetic and recreational interests in the land, and negatively affect Tidwell's Valley Club membership value. They also contended Parcel C was restricted to open space and recreational use.
defendant_argument: Defendants argued Plaintiffs lacked standing because they had no particularized interest in Parcel C, suffered no particularized injury, and their alleged harms were speculative and generalized. They maintained that community housing was an appropriate "public use."
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court vacated the district court's judgment, ruling that the Plaintiffs lacked standing to bring their claims, and remanded the case for entry of a dismissal.

title: State v. Bell
description: Whether the collective knowledge doctrine allows a police officer to make a warrantless arrest for a misdemeanor DUI committed outside the officer's personal presence, even if probable cause is established through information from another officer.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the "in the presence of the arresting officer" requirement for warrantless misdemeanor arrests can be satisfied by the collective knowledge of multiple officers, even if the arresting officer did not personally witness the offense.
defendant_argument: Bell argued that a warrantless arrest for a completed misdemeanor DUI, where the arresting officer did not personally witness the offense, violates Article I, section 17 of the Idaho Constitution, regardless of collective probable cause.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the district court's decision to reverse the magistrate court's denial of Bell's motion to suppress, ruling that a warrantless arrest for a misdemeanor DUI committed outside the arresting officer's presence is unconstitutional.

title: Bradbury v. City of Lewiston
description: Whether the City of Lewiston's interdepartmental fund transfers, street impact fees, payments to private entities, and water allocation to a golf course were unconstitutional or unlawful, with the plaintiff arguing they were illegal and the defendant arguing they were lawful.
plaintiff_argument: The City collected excessive utility fees, improperly spent municipal funds, made unconstitutional interdepartmental transfers, imposed illegal street impact fees, made improper donations to private entities, and provided 'free water' to a golf course at ratepayers' expense.
defendant_argument: The City's interdepartmental transfers were lawful, street impact fees were consistent with other municipalities, payments to private entities were for contracted services, and Bradbury lacked standing to challenge water allocation.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed in part and reversed in part, finding that street impact fees were an illegal tax and recovery was not barred by ITCA, but denied a refund as the plaintiff was not seeking one. All other claims against the City were affirmed in the City's favor.

title: Idaho Power Co. v. Idaho State Tax Commission
description: Whether the Idaho State Tax Commission's assessment of operating property for Idaho Power Company and Avista Corporation violated constitutional uniformity requirements, specifically concerning adjustments made for railroad property under federal law (4-R Act) and comparisons to other commercial property.
plaintiff_argument: The Companies argued that their operating property was unconstitutionally assessed at a higher percentage of its actual cash value than both railroad operating property (due to 4-R Act adjustments not applied to them) and other commercial property, violating Idaho's constitutional uniformity requirements.
defendant_argument: The Commission argued that the federal 4-R Act preempted Idaho's constitutional uniformity requirement as applied to railroads, and that its assessments complied with state rules (Rule 131) for other commercial property, thus not violating uniformity.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the district court's dismissal of the Companies' 4-R claim, finding that the 4-R Act does not preempt Idaho's constitutional uniformity requirement, and affirmed the district court's denial of summary judgment to the Commission on the Companies' alternative claim, allowing that claim to proceed to trial.

title: State v. Pool
description: Whether the search of a probationer's residence violated the Idaho Constitution because she only waived her Fourth Amendment rights against unlawful searches and seizures, but not her rights under Article I, section 17 of the Idaho Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that Pool's waiver of her Fourth Amendment rights constituted consent to warrantless searches, and that the Fourth Amendment and Idaho Constitution Article I, section 17 rights are coextensive, meaning the waiver covered both.
defendant_argument: Pool argued that she only waived her Fourth Amendment rights, not her rights under Article I, section 17 of the Idaho Constitution, and that these are separate rights requiring separate waivers.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the district court's decision, concluding that Pool's waiver of Fourth Amendment rights constituted consent to the warrantless search of her residence, as the state and federal constitutional protections were coextensive in this instance.

title: Planned Parenthood Great Northwest v. State
description: Whether the Idaho Constitution implicitly protects a fundamental right to abortion, thereby limiting the legislature's power to enact laws concerning public health, welfare, and safety related to abortion.
plaintiff_argument: The Idaho Constitution implicitly guarantees a fundamental right to abortion through various provisions (Article I, sections 1, 17, and 21), making the challenged abortion bans unconstitutional and subject to strict scrutiny. They also argue the laws violate equal protection, due process, special laws provision, separation of powers, and informational privacy, and are limited by the Idaho Human Rights Act.
defendant_argument: The Idaho Constitution does not implicitly contain a fundamental right to abortion, as such a right is not "deeply rooted" in Idaho's history and traditions at the time the Constitution was adopted. Therefore, the challenged laws are constitutional under rational-basis review.
decision_outcome: The court denied the petitioners' requests for extraordinary writs of prohibition and declaratory relief, dismissing the petitions with prejudice, and upheld the Total Abortion Ban, 6-Week Ban, and Civil Liability Law as constitutional.

title: State v. Lancaster
description: Whether the failure of arresting officers to inform a suspect of the cause of his arrest, as required by Idaho Code section 19-608, constitutes a constitutional violation under Article I, Section 17 of the Idaho Constitution that warrants the suppression of evidence.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the violation of Idaho Code section 19-608's notice requirements does not rise to a constitutional level and therefore does not require the suppression of evidence, citing precedent that statutory violations do not automatically equate to constitutional ones.
defendant_argument: Lancaster argued that the officers' failure to comply with Idaho Code section 19-608 rendered his arrest an unreasonable seizure under Article I, Section 17 of the Idaho Constitution, and thus his confession and other evidence should have been suppressed.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the district court's decision to deny the motion to suppress, concluding that the statutory violation of Idaho Code section 19-608 did not rise to a constitutional level.

title: State v. Pizzuto
description: Whether Idaho Code section 20-1016, which grants the Governor authority to approve or disapprove the Commission of Pardons and Parole's recommendation for commutation in death penalty cases, is constitutional.
plaintiff_argument: Pizzuto argued that Idaho Code section 20-1016 is unconstitutional because Article IV, section 7 of the Idaho Constitution places the commutation power exclusively with the Commission, and the Governor lacked authority to overrule its determination.
defendant_argument: The State of Idaho argued that Idaho Code section 20-1016 is constitutional, as the 1986 Amendment to Article IV, section 7 granted the Legislature the power to determine how and when commutations and pardons can be provided, and the statute properly reflects that authority.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the district court's orders, concluding that Idaho Code section 20-1016 is constitutional and remanding the cases for further proceedings.

title: State v. Riley
description: Whether police deviations from the initial purpose of a traffic stop unlawfully prolonged the stop, thereby violating the defendant's Fourth Amendment rights against unreasonable seizure.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the brief deviations during the traffic stop, including questioning about contraband and a conversation with backup officers, did not unlawfully prolong the stop because the drug dog alerted and established reasonable suspicion for a new crime before the original traffic stop's mission was completed.
defendant_argument: Riley argued that the police officer's deviations from the initial purpose of the traffic stop unconstitutionally prolonged her seizure, violating her Fourth Amendment rights, and therefore the evidence obtained should be suppressed.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Idaho reversed the district court's order that granted Riley's motion to suppress evidence, concluding that the deviations did not unlawfully prolong the traffic stop.

title: State v. Poe
description: Whether the Industrial Commission has standing to independently seek renewal of a restitution order in a criminal case.
plaintiff_argument: The Industrial Commission argued it has standing to renew the restitution order, asserting that crime victims have a constitutional right to restitution and that the Legislature intended for victims to be able to renew such judgments.
defendant_argument: The defendant did not actively argue in this appeal, but the lower courts, whose decisions were affirmed, found that the Industrial Commission lacked standing because victims are not parties to a criminal case and a restitution order is part of a criminal sentence that only the court or state can alter or renew.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the district court's decision, ruling that the Industrial Commission does not have standing to pursue a renewal of an order of restitution in a criminal case.

title: Pentico v. Idaho Commission for Reapportionment
description: Whether the Idaho Commission for Reapportionment timely filed its congressional redistricting plan and final report, and whether the adopted plan (Plan C03) violates Idaho Code by splitting local precinct boundary lines.
plaintiff_argument: The Commission failed to timely file its plan and report, and Plan C03 illegally splits local precinct boundaries, which is disruptive to the electoral process.
defendant_argument: The Commission timely filed its plan and report, and Plan C03's precinct splitting is permissible under an escape clause in Idaho Code section 72-1506(7) for both legislative and congressional plans.
decision_outcome: The court denied Pentico's request for a writ of prohibition, ruling that the Commission timely filed its report and that Plan C03 does not violate Idaho Code section 72-1506(7).

title: Durst v. Idaho Commission for Reapportionment
description: Whether Plan L03, the legislative redistricting plan, is constitutional under the Federal and Idaho Constitutions, with petitioners arguing it is unconstitutional and respondents arguing it is constitutional.
plaintiff_argument: Petitioners argue that Plan L03 violates the Idaho Constitution because it divides more counties than necessary to comply with the Equal Protection Clause, fails to preserve communities of interest, and results in oddly shaped districts, proposing alternative plans that split fewer counties.
defendant_argument: Respondents argue that Plan L03 complies with federal and state constitutional requirements, and that the Commission reasonably determined the number of county divisions needed for equal protection, rejecting petitioners' alternative plans as deficient.
decision_outcome: The court denied the petitioners' requests to issue a writ of prohibition, thereby upholding Plan L03.

title: State v. Randall
description: Whether a police officer's drug-detection dog trespassing into a stopped car during a drug trafficking investigation without a warrant, probable cause, or consent constitutes an unconstitutional search under the Fourth Amendment.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the initial traffic stop was justified, reasonable suspicion of drug trafficking developed, and the drug dog's entry into the car was instinctive, thus not constituting a search under the Fourth Amendment.
defendant_argument: Randall argued that the traffic stop was unconstitutionally prolonged due to lack of reasonable suspicion, and the drug dog's entry into his car before probable cause was established violated his Fourth Amendment rights as an unconstitutional search.
decision_outcome: The district court's denial of Randall's motion to suppress was reversed, and Randall's conviction was vacated.

title: Reclaim Idaho & the Commission to Protect & Preserve the Idaho Constitution, Inc. v. Denney
description: Whether recent limitations imposed by the Idaho Legislature on the people's initiative and referendum rights unconstitutionally infringe upon these rights.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the new signature threshold (SB 1110) and the delayed effective date for initiatives (Idaho Code section 34-1813(2)(a)) violate the people's constitutional initiative and referendum rights, effectively nullifying their power to legislate directly.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the challenged provisions are a lawful exercise of the legislature's constitutionally-delegated power to prescribe the conditions and manner under which initiatives and referenda may be carried out, and that the issues raised were nonjusticiable political questions.
decision_outcome: The court dismissed Gilmore's petition for lack of standing but granted Reclaim Idaho and the Committee's petition, declaring Idaho Code section 34-1805(2) (35-district signature requirement) and section 34-1813(2)(a) (delayed effective date) unconstitutional, restoring the previous 18-district requirement for section 34-1805(2).

title: State v. Amstutz
description: Whether a warrantless arrest for a completed misdemeanor DUI, where the arresting officer did not personally verify the felony status at the time of arrest, violates the defendant's constitutional rights against unreasonable searches and seizures.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the warrantless arrest was lawful under the collective knowledge doctrine, as dispatch's knowledge of Amstutz's prior DUI convictions, combined with the officer's observations, provided probable cause for a felony DUI, regardless of whether the officer personally recalled the felony status at the moment of arrest.
defendant_argument: Amstutz argued her warrantless arrest was unlawful because it was for a completed misdemeanor offense that occurred outside the officer's presence, violating her Idaho constitutional rights under State v. Clarke, and that the officer lacked sufficient personal knowledge at the time of arrest to establish probable cause for a felony DUI.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the district court's denial of Amstutz's motion to suppress, vacated her judgment of conviction, and remanded the case, finding her warrantless arrest for a completed misdemeanor DUI was unlawful.

title: State v. Sutterfield
description: Whether the district court erred in suppressing evidence obtained from a search incident to a citizen's arrest, where the arresting officer failed to fully comply with statutory notice requirements, and whether this failure transformed the arrest into an unconstitutional warrantless arrest by a peace officer.
plaintiff_argument: The State argues that Sutterfield was arrested by a private person and his agent, and the officer's failure to fully comply with statutory notice requirements did not rise to the level of a constitutional violation, thus suppression of evidence was inappropriate.
defendant_argument: Sutterfield argues that his arrest was an unlawful warrantless arrest by a peace officer for a completed misdemeanor, violating his constitutional rights, and therefore the evidence obtained from the search incident to that arrest should be suppressed.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reverses the district court's order suppressing evidence and dismissing the felony count of possession of a controlled substance, remanding the case for further proceedings.

title: State v. Heath
description: Whether drug paraphernalia, seized during an unlawful search and deemed contraband, must be returned to the defendant, and whether Idaho's prohibition of marijuana violates constitutional rights, including religious liberty.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the seized pipe and bong are contraband and should not be returned, and that the prohibition of marijuana is a valid exercise of state power that does not violate constitutional rights, including religious liberty.
defendant_argument: Heath argued that the pipe and bong must be returned because the evidence was suppressed due to an unlawful search, and that marijuana is not properly classified as a controlled substance and its prohibition infringes on his religious liberty.
decision_outcome: The Idaho Supreme Court affirmed the district court's decision, which upheld the magistrate court's denial of Heath's motion for the return of the pipe and bong, concluding that contraband is not returnable and the marijuana prohibition does not violate religious liberty.

title: Reagan v. Idaho Transportation Department
description: Whether Idaho Code section 49-1405(1)(b), which permits warrantless arrests for misdemeanor DUI committed outside an officer's presence, violates the Idaho Constitution, and if so, whether evidence obtained from such an unlawful arrest is admissible in an administrative license suspension hearing.
plaintiff_argument: Reagan argued that her warrantless arrest for DUI, which the officer did not witness, was unlawful under the Idaho Constitution, making the subsequent breathalyzer test results inadmissible for her license suspension.
defendant_argument: The Idaho Transportation Department argued that Idaho Code section 49-1405(1)(b) authorized the warrantless arrest for DUI, and that the breathalyzer test results were admissible in an administrative license suspension hearing regardless of the arrest's legality.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the district court's decision, holding that Idaho Code section 49-1405(1)(b) violates the Idaho Constitution and that the breathalyzer test, administered incident to an unlawful arrest, yielded inadmissible evidence for the administrative license suspension.

title: Gomersall v. St. Luke's Regional Medican Center, Ltd.
description: Whether Idaho Code section 5-230, which establishes an eight-year limitations period for minors to bring medical malpractice claims, is constitutional under due process and equal protection clauses, and whether the doctrine of equitable estoppel should prevent the defendant from asserting a statute of limitations defense.
plaintiff_argument: The Gomersalls argue that Idaho Code section 5-230 is unconstitutional, violating W.G.G.'s due process and equal protection rights by failing to toll the statute of limitations for medical malpractice claims until the age of majority, and that equitable estoppel should preclude SLRMC's statute of limitations defense due to their misleading communication.
defendant_argument: SLRMC argues that the Gomersalls' medical malpractice action is time-barred under Idaho Code sections 5-219(4) and 5-230, that section 5-230 is constitutional, and that the doctrine of equitable estoppel does not apply because no false representation of a material fact was made.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the district court's decision, granting summary judgment in favor of St. Luke's Regional Medical Center, finding that Idaho Code section 5-230 is constitutional and equitable estoppel does not apply.
